scope: Claim-level acidic/neutral cannabinoid chemistry, decarboxylation, degradation, genotype-by-environment, developmental sampling, trichome-color, and analytical-sampling evidence for THC-ENC-234 through THC-ENC-240.
rules: Analytical platform, sample preparation, tissue position, moisture basis, and calculation convention must remain explicit in cannabinoid claims.
Storage/degradation results remain bounded to tested matrices, temperatures, light conditions, sample forms, chemovars, and analytical methods.
Visual trichome observations can support local staging but do not replace chemical analysis or define a universal harvest threshold.
All mappings remain pending independent science review.

claimEvidence.supportedClaim: Acidic and neutral cannabinoids are analytically distinct forms, and sample preparation plus analytical method influence how those forms are measured and reported.
claimEvidence.sourceLocator: Wang et al. 2016 analytical/decarboxylation study; USP cannabis quality-attributes paper on representative sampling and validated analytical procedures.
claimEvidence.applicability: Supports separate acidic/neutral analytes, explicit analytical platform, and method-aware total-cannabinoid calculations.
claimEvidence.limitations: Regulatory reporting formulas vary by jurisdiction; scientific interpretation should preserve the measured analytes and method rather than infer one universal reporting convention.

claimEvidence.supportedClaim: Cannabinoid-acid decarboxylation changes with time and temperature and differs among THCA, CBDA, and CBGA, so one fixed time/temperature conversion rule cannot be assumed across cannabinoids and matrices.
claimEvidence.sourceLocator: Wang et al. 2016 kinetic experiments and analyte-recovery results.
claimEvidence.applicability: Supports condition-specific decarboxylation chemistry and explicit evidence limits.
claimEvidence.limitations: The tested matrix and laboratory conditions do not authorize a universal operational recipe; product recovery and degradation behavior can differ in other matrices and atmospheres.

claimEvidence.supportedClaim: Cannabis phytocannabinoid and terpenoid profiles change during storage in a manner dependent on time, temperature, matrix, and sample form, demonstrating that degradation cannot be represented by one universal chemical clock.
claimEvidence.sourceLocator: Milay et al. 2020 one-year storage experiment across whole/ground inflorescences, extracts, solvents, and temperatures.
claimEvidence.applicability: Supports condition-specific storage/degradation records and separation of observed compound changes from age estimation.
claimEvidence.limitations: The studied chemovars and storage systems do not define universal degradation rates for all cannabis products.

claimEvidence.supportedClaim: Cannabinoid concentration is influenced by genotype and environment, while tissue position and analytical/extraction method can also change the measured profile, so genotype effects must be interpreted within the tested environment and sampling method.
claimEvidence.sourceLocator: De Prato et al. 2022 controlled genotype/daylength/temperature/nitrogen experiments; Namdar et al. 2018 positional and extraction-method study.
claimEvidence.applicability: Supports genotype-by-environment interpretation and control of sampling/method confounders.
claimEvidence.limitations: Treatment effects apply to the studied germplasm and environments and should not be transferred as universal cannabinoid-response rules.

claimEvidence.supportedClaim: Cannabis trichome development is asynchronous and genotype/age-dependent, while cannabinoid measurements vary by inflorescence position, so developmental comparisons require repeated, position-defined sampling rather than a universal harvest week.
claimEvidence.sourceLocator: Punja, Sutton, and Kim 2023 trichome maturation study; Namdar et al. 2018 inflorescence-position chemistry study.
claimEvidence.limitations: Neither source establishes one universal cannabinoid peak date or harvest stage across genotypes.

claimEvidence.supportedClaim: Cannabis trichome color changes can accompany maturation and senescence, but storage chemistry and postharvest changes are condition-dependent; visual color therefore cannot be converted directly into one cannabinoid concentration or degradation state.
claimEvidence.sourceLocator: Punja, Sutton, and Kim 2023 color/autofluorescence/senescence observations; Milay et al. 2020 condition-dependent postharvest chemistry.
claimEvidence.applicability: Supports trichome color as a locally validated field observation rather than a chemical assay.
claimEvidence.limitations: Observer method, imaging conditions, tissue position, genotype, and storage context all limit transferability of visual thresholds.

claimEvidence.supportedClaim: Cannabis inflorescence is a chemically heterogeneous matrix requiring representative sampling, and within-plant position plus extraction/analytical method can materially alter measured cannabinoid and terpenoid composition.
claimEvidence.sourceLocator: USP cannabis quality-attributes paper; Namdar et al. 2018 positional/extraction-method findings.
claimEvidence.applicability: Supports representative batch sampling, sample-position records, validated analytical methods, and claims discipline.
claimEvidence.limitations: Specific acceptance limits, legal action thresholds, and regulatory sampling plans remain jurisdiction- and program-specific.
